passages.t: Everything swept away, beginning with Jerusalem
passages.happening:
‘This is the word of the LORD that came to Zephaniah son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah’ (verse 1).

God says he will sweep away everything from the face of the earth (verse 2): people and animals, birds and fish, the idols and their worshipers (verse 3). Then he turns to Judah and Jerusalem. He will cut off every remnant of Baal and the names of the idolatrous priests (verse 4), ‘those who bow on the rooftops to worship the host of heaven, those who bow down and swear by the LORD but also swear by Milcom’ (verse 5), and those who have turned back from following the LORD (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Josiah became king about 640 BC, at eight, after his father Amon was murdered. His grandfather Manasseh had reigned fifty-five years and filled Judah with foreign worship: altars to Baal, an Asherah pole in the temple, altars to the stars in the temple courts, and child sacrifice. Josiah's reform began, by 2 Chronicles, in his twelfth year, about 628 BC, and by 2 Kings centered on his eighteenth, about 622 BC, when the Book of the Law was found. Zephaniah 1 describes the practices that reform swept away.

Flat rooftops were used for many things, including worship of the sun, moon and stars, a practice linked with Assyrian influence. To swear by the LORD and by Milcom, a god of the Ammonites, was an attempt to keep the God of Israel while adding other gods.

The opening verses echo the flood and the order of creation in Genesis 1, run backwards: people, animals, birds, fish.
passages.later: Second Kings tells how Josiah removed the priests who burned incense to Baal and to the host of heaven (2 Kings 23:5) and pulled down the rooftop altars (2 Kings 23:12).
passages.hard:
Why does God threaten to sweep away all creation, animals included, when people are the ones who sinned?

The opening deliberately echoes the flood and the order of creation in Genesis 1, and the language is sweeping on purpose. Many interpreters read it as the prophets' way of saying how serious judgment is, rather than a literal prediction that all animals would die; the focus narrows at once to Judah and Jerusalem. Others point out that in the Bible human sin damages the whole creation, so judgment on humanity affects the world people were meant to care for. And the later chapters show that the purpose of judgment is not to wipe out but to purify: a remnant remains, and the nations come to worship.

Readers still feel the severity of the passage, and rightly so. It is not a key for reading any disaster today as God's verdict on the people it falls on.
passages.asks: The people swore by the LORD and by Milcom too. Ask what else you have sworn by beside God. And ask what it would mean to follow the LORD without turning back.

passages.t: Be silent: the day of the LORD's sacrifice
passages.happening:
‘Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD, for the Day of the LORD is near’ (verse 7). The LORD has prepared a sacrifice and set apart his guests. On that day he will punish the princes, the king's sons, and all who dress in foreign clothes (verse 8), and those who fill their master's house with violence and deceit (verse 9).

A cry will go up from the Fish Gate and the Second District (verse 10), and the merchants of the Hollow will be silenced (verse 11). ‘And at that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps and punish the men settled in complacency’ (verse 12), who say to themselves that the LORD will do nothing, good or bad. Their wealth will be plundered. They will build houses and not live in them, and plant vineyards and never drink the wine (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The sacrifice is Judah itself, and the guests are the invaders God has invited. Foreign clothes may mean royal officials who took on the dress of foreign courts or cults, a sign of divided loyalty. Leaping over the threshold is obscure; a Philistine temple custom of not stepping on the threshold is recorded in 1 Samuel, and some read this as a foreign practice taken up in Jerusalem.

The Fish Gate, the Second District and the Hollow were parts of Jerusalem, the last probably a market quarter in a valley where silver was weighed out for trade. God searching with lamps pictures a search that misses no one.

The complacent are the heart of the charge. They do not deny God; they think he does nothing, that he will neither help nor judge. The punishment is the covenant's warning: houses not lived in, vineyards not drunk.
passages.later: The law had warned: ‘You will build a house but will not live in it’ (Deuteronomy 28:30). A Philistine custom about the threshold is told in 1 Samuel 5:5.
passages.asks: The complacent believed God would do nothing. Ask where you have lived as if God were real but irrelevant. And ask what God would find if he searched your life with a lamp.

passages.t: The great Day: wrath and darkness
passages.happening:
‘The great Day of the LORD is near’ (verse 14), near and coming quickly. The warrior will cry out bitterly. ‘That day will be a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of destruction and desolation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness’ (verse 15), a day of trumpet and battle cry against fortified cities and corner towers (verse 16).

God will bring distress on people so that they walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the LORD (verse 17). The verse goes on to name the death of war, which these notes do not repeat. ‘Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the Day of the LORD’s wrath’ (verse 18). The whole earth will be consumed by the fire of his jealousy.
passages.hearers:
Verse 15 is built from a string of paired nouns, day after day, a drumbeat of dread. Its opening words in the Latin translation, Dies irae, became the first line of a famous medieval hymn of judgment.

The Day of the LORD in Zephaniah is God's decisive act. It fell on Jerusalem when Babylon destroyed it in 587 or 586 BC, and it also points to a final day of judgment. Silver and gold, which the merchants of verse 11 weighed out, cannot buy anyone out of it.

The fire of God's jealousy is his zeal for his people and his name, which will not share them with rival gods.
passages.later: Amos had warned that the Day of the LORD would be darkness and not light (Amos 5:18), and Joel called it ‘a day of darkness and gloom’ (Joel 2:2).
passages.asks: Silver and gold cannot rescue anyone on that day. Ask what you are counting on that could not help you before God. And ask how the seriousness of this day might make you more honest now.
